1.s: An Amalekite brings news of Saul’s death, claiming to have killed him, and David has him executed. David laments: “How the mighty have fallen!”
1.d: The Amalekite’s claim was false, since Saul had taken his own life; David had him killed for claiming to harm the LORD’s anointed [[tosn:2 Samuel 1:1–16]]. The lament comes from the Book of Jashar, a book of poems no longer available [[tosn:2 Samuel 1:18]].

2.s: David is anointed king over Judah at Hebron, while Saul’s son Ish-bosheth rules the north. Civil war begins.
2.d: David asked the LORD for guidance before moving [[tosn:2 Samuel 2:1]]. Judah, loyal to David, came into conflict with the other tribes, loyal to Ish-bosheth [[tosn:2 Samuel 2:1–32]].

3.s: David grows stronger. Abner defects to David but is murdered by Joab. David mourns him publicly.
3.d: The civil war probably lasted most of David’s seven years in Hebron [[tosn:2 Samuel 3:1]]. Abner, the real power among Saul’s supporters, changing sides was the turning point [[tosn:2 Samuel 3:1–39]].

4.s: Two men murder Ish-bosheth and bring his head to David, who executes them. Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth is introduced.
4.d: The murderers expected a reward, but David refused to reward betrayal [[tosn:2 Samuel 4:6]] [[tosn:2 Samuel 4:8]].

5.s: All Israel makes David king. He captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites and defeats the Philistines.
5.d: The Jebusites believed their city could not be captured [[tosn:2 Samuel 5:6]]. David’s choice of Jerusalem as Israel’s political and religious centre matters for the rest of the Bible [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

6.s: David brings the ark to Jerusalem, dancing with all his might. Uzzah dies touching it, and Michal despises David.
6.d: Bringing the ark to the new capital publicly honoured the LORD as Israel’s true king [[tosn:2 Samuel 6:1–23]]. Uzzah probably meant well, but touching the ark broke God’s command [[tosn:2 Samuel 6:6–7]] [[bible:Numbers 4:15]].

7.s: David wants to build God a house. Instead God promises to build David a house: a dynasty, and a son whose throne will be established forever.
7.d: God would build David a house, a dynasty that would last forever [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Hebrews 1:5 applies 7:14 to Jesus, and the promise is fulfilled in his eternal reign [[tosn:2 Samuel 7:14]] [[tosn:2 Samuel 7:19]]. See also Luke 1:32–33 [[bible:Luke 1:32-33]].

8.s: David defeats surrounding nations, and his officials are listed.
8.d: His victories enlarged the kingdom and he set up officials to govern it [[tosn:2 Samuel 8:1–18]]. In David’s time Israel’s borders reached from Egypt to the Euphrates, as promised to Abraham [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

9.s: David shows kindness to Mephibosheth for Jonathan’s sake, giving him a place at the king’s table.
9.d: “Kindness” here is covenant loyalty, kept because of his promise to Jonathan [[tosn:2 Samuel 9:1]]. Placed between battle reports, it shows David showing mercy as well as winning wars [[tosn:2 Samuel 9:1–13]].

10.s: The Ammonites humiliate David’s envoys, and war follows with Ammon and the Arameans.
10.d: David’s sin with Bathsheba happened during this successful war against the Ammonites [[tosn:2 Samuel 11:1–27]].

11.s: While his army is at war, David sleeps with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, then arranges Uriah’s death. “the thing that David had done displeased Yahweh.”
11.d: It shows David was capable of serious moral failure, which deeply damaged his life and rule [[tosn:2 Samuel 11:1–27]]. The text places the blame on David alone [[tosn:2 Samuel 11:4]]. Matthew names her in Jesus’s family tree as “her who had been Uriah’s wife” [[bible:Matthew 1:6]].

12.s: The prophet Nathan tells David a parable of a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb. “You are the man!” David repents, but the child dies. Solomon is born.
12.d: It is one of the few parables in the Old Testament [[tosn:2 Samuel 12:1]]. The story helped David see his sin [[bsn:2 Samuel 11:1–14:33]]. The title of Psalm 51 links it to this moment [[bible:Psalm 51]].

13.s: David’s son Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar, and her brother Absalom murders Amnon, then flees.
13.d: David was furious but does not seem to have punished Amnon [[tosn:2 Samuel 13:21]]. Nathan had warned of terrible trouble in David’s family [[bsn:2 Samuel 11:1–14:33]] [[bible:2 Samuel 12:10]].

14.s: Joab arranges Absalom’s return through a wise woman of Tekoa, but David will not see him for two years.
14.d: The woman argued that Absalom’s exile harmed the whole kingdom [[tosn:2 Samuel 14:13]], and that God “devises means, that he who is banished not be an outcast” [[bible:2 Samuel 14:14]].

15.s: Absalom wins the people’s hearts and leads a rebellion. David flees Jerusalem weeping, sending the ark back.
15.d: A chariot, horses and fifty runners were signs of kingship, as Samuel had warned [[tosn:2 Samuel 15:1]]. The title of Psalm 3 links it to this flight [[bible:Psalm 3]].

16.s: Shimei curses David as he flees, and David will not let him be killed. Absalom takes his father’s concubines.
16.d: Shimei blamed David for the deaths in Saul’s family [[tosn:2 Samuel 16:7–8]]. Absalom’s act on the roof mirrors David’s sin, which began on that roof, and fulfils Nathan’s warning [[tosn:2 Samuel 16:22]] [[bible:2 Samuel 12:11]].

17.s: Hushai, David’s friend, defeats Ahithophel’s advice to Absalom, and Ahithophel hangs himself.
17.d: Absalom rejected the good advice because the LORD was working against him [[tosn:2 Samuel 17:1–14]] [[bible:2 Samuel 17:14]]. This answers David’s prayer in 15:31 [[bible:2 Samuel 15:31]].

18.s: Absalom’s army is defeated, and he is killed while caught by his hair in a tree. David weeps: “My son Absalom! I wish I had died for you!”
18.d: Joab disobeyed David’s order to deal gently with Absalom [[tosn:2 Samuel 18:5]]. Absalom, proud of his hair, died because of it and had no proper burial [[tosn:2 Samuel 18:9]].

19.s: Joab rebukes David for mourning instead of thanking his army. David returns to Jerusalem, pardoning Shimei and Mephibosheth.
19.d: This is the only time Joab openly corrects David [[tosn:2 Samuel 19:5–7]]. Quarrels between the northern tribes and Judah break out over his return [[bible:2 Samuel 19:41-43]].

20.s: Sheba leads a northern revolt; Joab murders his rival Amasa and ends the revolt.
20.d: The cry “We have no portion in David” is used again when the north breaks away from Solomon’s son [[tosn:2 Samuel 20:1]] [[bible:1 Kings 12:16]].

21.s: David atones for Saul’s killing of the Gibeonites, and his warriors defeat Philistine giants.
21.d: The famine came because Saul broke the oath made to the Gibeonites [[tosn:2 Samuel 21:1]] [[bible:Joshua 9:19-20]]. Chapters 21–24 are arranged by topic, not by time [[tosn:2 Samuel 21:1–24:25]].

22.s: David’s song of thanksgiving: “Yahweh is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.”
22.d: The same song is in Psalm 18, and David probably sang it much earlier in life [[tosn:2 Samuel 22:1–51]].

23.s: David’s last words, and the list of his mighty men, ending with Uriah the Hittite.
23.d: These were his last public act of worship as king, not necessarily his final words [[tosn:2 Samuel 23:1]]. The very last name on the list is Uriah the Hittite [[tosn:2 Samuel 23:39]].

24.s: David orders a census, God sends a plague, and David buys a threshing floor to build an altar.
24.d: Araunah’s threshing floor later became the site of the temple [[tosn:2 Samuel 24:16]] [[bible:2 Chronicles 3:1]]. David will not offer God what “cost me nothing” [[bible:2 Samuel 24:24]].
